label: 03 Sep 2026
summary: Sparse attention moved closer to a full serving primitive: Faster Flash Decoding fuses low-bit scanning, adaptive block selection, and refinement, while llama.cpp lands model-directed sparse FlashAttention for DeepSeek-V4 and GLM.
Model-specific fusion is paying measurable end-to-end dividends: vLLM's Qwen3.8 Flash-Next PLE kernels improve median TTFT by 5.5–8.5% and per-user decode rate by 2.9–4.5% on TP4 GB300.
Speculative paths are being optimized beyond the target model: SGLang prunes unused draft LM-head rows, and llama.cpp eliminates an RDNA register-spill cliff in eight-token verification.

Memory movement remains a first-class latency problem across scales: mzCache overlaps mobile restoration with GPU inference, while TensorRT-LLM pipelines disaggregated KV transfer behind chunked prefill.
Correct configuration dominates confidentiality cost on Blackwell: a revised controlled study finds roughly 1–3% throughput overhead after framework fixes, versus 30–40% for stock overlap paths.
Quantization work is shifting from local reconstruction toward end-to-end objectives: REAL-Q dynamically refreshes an output-distribution-aligned surrogate after each column block.

items.title: Faster Than Flash: Exploiting Attention Sparsity for Efficient Long-Context Decoding
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Faster Flash Decoding fuses 2-bit content scanning, top-delta block selection, and selective refinement, reaching 87.0 tok/s at 16K on H100 versus 44.5 tok/s for FlashAttention-2 in the reported batch-one study.
items.problem: Exact decode attention reloads the full KV cache for every token, while existing sparse methods either maintain auxiliary metadata, impose a fixed top-k budget, or pay global synchronization for adaptive selection.
items.why_it_matters: At long context and small decode batches, KV reads dominate latency; a selector that costs too much or stores substantial metadata can erase the sparsity benefit.
items.existing_approaches: FlashAttention-2 remains exact and bandwidth-linear in context length. Quest and SparQ use metadata and fixed budgets; Twilight adapts selection through a global softmax; conventional KV quantizers usually dequantize before attention.
items.limitations: Selection is approximate, quality depends on the top-delta threshold and pseudo-max assumption, and the reported end-to-end experiments are batch one with context lengths up to 16K even though kernel tests extend to 256K.
items.proposed_solution: Store each key as a 2-bit thumbnail plus an 8-bit residual, estimate a pseudo-maximum from sink and local tokens, scan blocks with a top-delta threshold, and refine only selected keys inside a fused Triton pipeline.
items.key_differences: The quantized scan is both the importance metric and reusable compute, avoiding a separate index structure; top-delta adapts cardinality without top-p's global reduction.
items.results_with_conditions: PyTorch 2.8, Triton 3.4, CUDA 12.8. RTX 4090 kernel test, batch 1, 4K–256K: delta=5 averaged 7.33× versus PyTorch SDPA/FlashAttention-2, with 0.17 ms versus 1.12 ms at 256K. End-to-end Llama-3.1-8B-style evaluation at 16K: RTX 4090 51.8 tok/s versus 21.9 tok/s dense (2.37×); H100 87.0 versus 44.5 tok/s (1.96×). Quest reached 47.8 and 73.5 tok/s respectively. Precision is a 2-bit key thumbnail plus 8-bit residual; values remain available for selected blocks.
items.assessment: High technical value and worth deep reading or reproduction. The fused selector-compute design is credible and code is public, but production validation should add mixed request lengths, continuous batching, tail latency, and quality stress tests beyond the published thresholds.

items.title: mzCache: On-Device LLM Memory Management under Multitasking
items.one_sentence_takeaway: mzCache turns forced mobile-memory eviction into an overlapped restoration pipeline, cutting TTFT by 2.1–5.5× versus storage-backed partial offload across two phones, two models, and 8K–32K contexts.
items.problem: Mobile multitasking can evict model weights and KV state while an on-device assistant is idle, forcing a later request to reload storage or recompute the context before producing its first token.
items.why_it_matters: Weights plus a long-context KV cache can consume 5–7 GB on a 12 GB phone; the paper observes a user-visible TTFT jump from 0.8 seconds to 16 seconds after eviction.
items.existing_approaches: Android paging compresses anonymous KV pages into zRAM and restores on page faults, while a partial-offload runtime reloads evicted layers from storage before GPU prefill.
items.limitations: OS paging poorly compresses KV state and can trigger cascading page faults; partial offload serializes restoration before inference. mzCache currently handles one context, relies on offline throughput profiles, and assumes dense models touch all weights and KV state.
items.proposed_solution: Partition model state into fine-grained shared buffers, use unified memory for GPU execution while CPU cores restore concurrently, split evicted data between compressed-memory and storage paths, and evict in backward order so near-term layers return first.
items.key_differences: The system optimizes recovery from an externally imposed and unknown eviction amount rather than managing a known oversubscription plan during steady-state inference.
items.results_with_conditions: Android llama.cpp prototype on Galaxy S25+ and OnePlus 12; Qwen3-0.6B and EXAONE-4.0-1.2B; accumulated contexts 8K, 16K, and 32K plus an 8-token follow-up. Across 0%, 25%, 50%, and 75% remaining memory, TTFT improves 2.1–5.5× over layer-granular storage-backed partial offload. At full eviction it is 2.5–3.0× faster than OS paging on Galaxy S25+ and 9.2–25.9× on OnePlus 12. Precision and generation concurrency were not reported in the primary source.
items.assessment: High practical value for persistent mobile assistants and worth deep reading. The evaluation is unusually realistic, but multi-context coordination, thermal adaptation, MoE activation prediction, and sparse-attention restoration remain open.

items.title: Benchmarking Confidential Computing Performance on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs
items.one_sentence_takeaway: A controlled B200 study localizes confidential-inference overhead to encrypted host operations and NVLink traffic, showing about 1–3% throughput cost with patched frameworks instead of the 30–40% seen in stock overlap paths.
items.problem: Confidential-computing overhead is commonly reported as one aggregate slowdown even though fixed encrypted command/readback cost and NVLink encryption scale differently with batch, topology, and framework scheduling.
items.why_it_matters: Operators need to protect prompts, KV state, and weights without buying excess capacity based on avoidable software stalls or assuming a low-overhead result transfers to a different parallelism strategy.
items.existing_approaches: Stock stacks encrypt PCIe traffic, command submission, and NVLink collectives but may force token readback synchronous, destroying compute/copy overlap; comparisons across different hosts or configurations obscure the cause.
items.limitations: The study accepts the security boundary rather than auditing it, covers one eight-B200 host, and excludes cross-node RDMA, disaggregated serving, attestation, and confidential-VM startup.
items.proposed_solution: Use paired CC-on/off runs on identical hardware, decompose cost into per-host-operation and encrypted-collective terms, predict serving loss with microbenchmarks, and patch frameworks with asynchronous device-to-host handling.
items.key_differences: It reports a performance surface across model, concurrency, sequence length, and parallelism, then validates the causal mechanism end to end instead of publishing one platform average.
items.results_with_conditions: Dual-socket Intel Xeon 6767P, 8× NVIDIA B200, Ubuntu 24.04.3, driver 595.71.05; NVFP4, FP8, AWQ, and BF16 models. Stock SGLang 0.5.13 with Qwen3-8B BF16, TP1: CC reduced throughput 34.4–38.9% at concurrency 16–64; at c64 TPOT rose 5.48→8.28 ms and TTFT 259→409 ms. With asynchronous-D2H/SGLang fixes, Qwen2.5-72B-AWQ TP1 showed −0.2% to +0.6% across c1–c32 for 1024-in/256-out, and a 1.2% median penalty across ten c32 shapes, worst 6.5% at 4096-in/1024-out.
items.assessment: High-value operational study and worth deep reading for secure inference. Its strongest lesson is configuration sensitivity; reproduce on the intended model, TP/EP layout, and host path before capacity planning.

items.title: vLLM: Fuse Qwen3.8 Flash-Next PLE Kernels
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Fusing n-gram IDs, dilated short convolution, and the PLE gate removes tiny-op and temporary-buffer overhead, improving median TTFT by 5.5–8.5% and decode rate by 2.9–4.5% on TP4 GB300.
items.problem: Qwen3.8 Flash-Next's PLE path performed n-gram construction, short convolution, gating, and key/value projections through multiple eager or compiled operations with avoidable launches and intermediate tensors.
items.why_it_matters: These small operations repeat on every decode and speculative step; even dramatic microkernel gains matter only if they reduce full-model TTFT or TPOT under real concurrency.
items.existing_approaches: The n-gram and short-convolution paths used eager custom operations, while the PLE gate went through torch.compile; separate K/V projections and mixed-batch gather/scatter added more traffic.
items.limitations: The optimized production path is NVIDIA-specific, measured on GB300 for one Qwen model, and the largest microbenchmark speedups should not be generalized beyond the exact shapes.
items.proposed_solution: Replace the PLE primitives with Triton kernels, fuse n-gram generation, dilated convolution, and gate work where possible, merge K/V projections, and preserve speculative-state rollback and ragged request semantics.
items.key_differences: The change explicitly validates integer overflow, EOS crossing, causal cache writes, mixed speculative batches, and BF16 numerical parity while reporting both kernel and serving-level measurements.
items.results_with_conditions: 4× GB300, TP4, Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, 8K input / 1K output speed-bench, concurrency 1/4/16/64, prefix caching and FlashInfer autotune disabled. Median TTFT fell 184.31→172.31, 216.74→198.27, 223.82→209.72, and 245.79→232.24 ms. Median reciprocal TPOT rose 234.00→244.61, 170.58→177.43, 97.39→100.18, and 46.00→47.59 tok/s. GB300 microbenchmarks report 28–41× for n-gram IDs, 1.38–3.47× versus compiled PLE gate, and 5.83–12.07× for short convolution.
items.assessment: High production value and worth reproducing for Qwen3.8 Flash-Next. The end-to-end gains are modest but well contextualized, while memory savings were asserted without a quantified peak-memory table.

items.title: SGLang: Prune Unused EAGLE Draft-Extend Logits
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Projecting only verifier-consumed draft rows cuts the EAGLE draft-extend graph by 12.4% and raises matched-context output throughput by 2.45% on 4×GB300.
items.problem: During EAGLE draft extension under CUDA graphs, SGLang projected full-vocabulary logits for every draft row although the verifier consumed only selected per-request rows.
items.why_it_matters: The unnecessary LM-head work and output copy sit directly on the speculative decode critical path and consume graph-capture memory.
items.existing_approaches: The prior graph kept a simple full-row logits contract, paying projection and copy cost for rows used only to evolve hidden and speculative state.
items.limitations: The optimization owns only the draft-extend graph; four full-vocabulary projections in draft-decode remain. The main measurement is an engine-side fixed-batch generation window, not service-level AIPerf.
items.proposed_solution: Keep all six draft rows through the model to preserve state evolution, select the verifier-consumed rows immediately before the LM head, and size the graph logits buffer to those rows.
items.key_differences: Compute is pruned at the last safe point, so hidden-state evolution and the output contract remain unchanged while only expensive vocabulary projection shrinks.
items.results_with_conditions: Qwen3.5-397B-A17B-NVFP4, one node with 4×GB300, TP4/DP4/EP4, FP8 KV, NEXTN with five speculative steps/six draft tokens, CUDA graphs, fixed batch 28, one 88,786-token prompt repeated over 112 requests, exact OSL 860, temperature 0. Target-step host time fell 29.689→28.997 ms (−2.33%); exact-context output rate rose 4,542.5→4,654.0 tok/s/GPU (+2.45%). Draft-extend graph fell 1.113→0.975 ms (−12.44%) and capture memory 0.15→0.07 GB. Natural-acceptance runs completed 112/112 in both arms; mean acceptance length shifted 3.684→3.653.
items.assessment: A precise and well-measured speculative-path optimization. Worth deep reading for EAGLE implementers; reproduce with production replenishment and end-to-end request latency before extrapolating the 2.45% engine gain.

items.title: llama.cpp: Model-Directed Sparse FlashAttention for DeepSeek-V4 and GLM
items.one_sentence_takeaway: A live-KV hint lets llama.cpp skip inactive attention entries, scaling from negligible gains at short context to 2.20× prompt throughput and 1.56× generation throughput at a 1M-token offset on DGX Spark.
items.problem: DeepSeek-V4 and GLM expose sparse-attention structure, but generic FlashAttention still scans the full KV range because the backend lacks a bound on live entries per query token.
items.why_it_matters: The unnecessary KV scan grows with context and dominates local long-context inference, especially on bandwidth-limited integrated systems.
items.existing_approaches: The earlier sparse prototype embedded more model-specific logic; dense FlashAttention ignored model sparsity. Fixed external indices would complicate future QSA-style mechanisms.
items.limitations: Results come from a 2.0625-bpw DeepSeek-V4 quantization on one DGX Spark; the benefit is near zero below roughly 8K and the PR explicitly asks for broader testing.
items.proposed_solution: Pass a model-level hint for the maximum live KV entries per token into ggml/CUDA and use it to gather only relevant cache entries before the FlashAttention computation.
items.key_differences: The backend receives a compact capacity hint rather than implementing the model's selector, making the same mechanism extensible to other sparse schemes such as Qwen QSA.
items.results_with_conditions: DGX Spark, DeepSeek-V4 IQ2_XXS at 2.0625 bpw. llama-bench pp2048: 563.31→563.53 tok/s at zero offset, 389.50→461.63 at 32K, 204.63→315.26 at 131K, and 33.99→74.90 at 1M (2.20×). tg32: 19.00→19.07 tok/s at zero offset, 14.20→15.73 at 131K, and 5.31→8.30 at 1M (1.56×). Batch/concurrency and KV precision beyond the model quantization were not reported in the primary source.
items.assessment: High practical value for extremely long local contexts and worth reproduction. The crossover is the key result: it is not a universal short-context speedup, and correctness/quality needs broader workload testing.

items.title: llama.cpp: Remove the IQ3_S Vulkan Register-Spill Cliff
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Restructuring eight-column IQ3_S mat-vec avoids 442 spilled VGPRs and lifts controlled Qwen3.8-27B eight-token verification from 67.6 to 77.0 tok/s on Radeon 8060S.
items.problem: At NUM_COLS=8, used by wide speculative verification, the IQ3_S Vulkan shader exhausted RDNA's vector-register budget and spilled 17 KB per wave, making the kernel nine times slower than the four-column case.
items.why_it_matters: A single rare quantized tensor type can stall a whole speculative verification graph, so model-level speed can collapse even when most layers scale normally.
items.existing_approaches: The shader kept 256 B values plus temporaries live while the compiler grouped memory loads, exceeding the practical VGPR budget; other IQ and K quant types did not show this cliff.
items.limitations: Only IQ3_S at batch/column counts above four is affected, model-level gains depend on how many IQ3_S tensors a quantized checkpoint contains, and speculative throughput varied with acceptance.
items.proposed_solution: Change the shader's work decomposition so the eight-column path reports 252 VGPRs with zero spills and zero scratch instead of 256 VGPRs plus 442 spilled registers.
items.key_differences: The fix targets register lifetime rather than arithmetic count and includes shader-stat, isolated graph, model throughput, perplexity, and checkpoint-composition evidence.
items.results_with_conditions: Radeon 8060S Graphics, RADV STRIX_HALO, m=4096, k=14336: IQ3_S n=8 fell from 1,589.0 µs to the spill-free path; the PR reports 252 VGPRs, 0 spill, 0 scratch after the fix. Qwen3.8-27B UD-Q4_K_M, four IQ3_S tensors: deterministic llama-bench pp8 improved 67.6→77.0 tok/s; tg32 12.4→12.6; DFlash2 n_max=7 moved from 31.3/31.8/34.9 to 34.5/35.2/35.3 tok/s across variable-acceptance runs. An IQ3_S-heavy checkpoint cut WikiText-2 wall time 714.3→283.2 s with statistically unchanged perplexity.
items.assessment: Excellent diagnosis of a hardware-specific performance cliff and worth reproducing on RDNA Vulkan. It is a surgical fix, not a general quantization speedup; report checkpoint tensor composition when citing model-level gains.

items.title: FlashInfer: Make NCCL Expert-Parallel Dispatch CUDA-Graph Capturable
items.one_sentence_takeaway: A persistent, rebindable NCCL-EP handle and capture-stream routing turn FlashInfer's split expert-parallel path from first-replay failure into validated graph replay for both low-latency and high-throughput algorithms.
items.problem: The split NCCL expert-parallel path created and destroyed a native handle inside every forward; CUDA graphs captured freed pointers, and transport work from a persistent handle could silently execute on the wrong stream.
items.why_it_matters: MoE serving relies on CUDA graphs to suppress launch overhead, but a capture that succeeds and crashes or becomes a no-op only on replay can escape ordinary correctness tests.
items.existing_approaches: Eager execution recreated a combined Init+Update handle each step. Simply moving creation outside capture still left per-step routing stale and operations on the creation-time stream.
items.limitations: The merged change is an enablement/correctness fix rather than a speed result; the vLLM consumer still requires a follow-up and compatible FlashInfer release.
items.proposed_solution: Create one durable handle before capture, record a per-step update that rebinds routing without allocation, and dispatch/complete on the active capture stream while preserving explicit non-graph stream behavior.
items.key_differences: Tests mutate top-k IDs between replays and inspect transport routing, catching the silent-no-op case that output-only identity tests miss.
items.results_with_conditions: Reproduction before the fix: 4×B200, DP4, Qwen3-30B-A3B through vLLM flashinfer_ep_low_latency; eager completed at about 616 tok/s per rank, while both piecewise and full graph capture completed then faulted on first replay. After the fix, 4-rank low-latency and high-throughput capture/replay tests passed across changed routing; 72 mock-suite tests passed. Model batch, input/output lengths, precision, and post-fix end-to-end throughput were not reported in the primary source.
items.assessment: High correctness value and worth deep reading for EP/runtime engineers. Do not treat it as a performance claim until the consumer integration lands and a graph-versus-eager serving benchmark is published.

items.title: TensorRT-LLM: Pipeline KV Transfer Behind Chunked Prefill
items.one_sentence_takeaway: TensorRT-LLM now sends completed KV blocks after each prefill chunk so RDMA can overlap GPU prefill, leaving only the final slice on the generation critical path when the network keeps up.
items.problem: Disaggregated context servers previously waited for the entire prompt prefill to finish before sending a monolithic KV cache, serializing two large phases before decode could begin.
items.why_it_matters: For long prompts, TTFT includes both expensive prefill and large RDMA transfer; overlapping them can remove nearly all but the final chunk's transfer time.
items.existing_approaches: The Python NIXL transceiver posted one whole-request receive and one monolithic send. Bounce staging, pipeline parallelism, and recurrent-state caches assume request-wide ownership and are not compatible with incremental block transfer.
items.limitations: The opt-in path requires Python NIXL, PP=1, no bounce buffer, no Mamba/hybrid cache, chunked prefill, beam width 1, and generation-first scheduling. No latency, bandwidth, GPU, model, or end-to-end benchmark was reported in the primary source.
items.proposed_solution: Create one send task per completed block-aligned prefill slice within a request session, retain a monolithic receive allocation, signal completion on the final slice, and defer sliding-window groups until their final active window is known.
items.key_differences: Chunking is sender-only and preserves receiver protocol shape; session ownership, cancellation, prefix reuse, sliding-window addressing, and cross-rank quiescence are explicitly handled.
items.results_with_conditions: The merged PR reports unit coverage for chunk boundaries, prefix reuse, mixed full/SWA groups, cancellation, consensus, and bounded polling. Performance conditions and numeric results: Not reported in the primary source.
items.assessment: Architecturally important and worth deep reading for P/D disaggregation, but reproduction is essential because the expected overlap benefit depends on chunk size, prefill time, NIXL/RDMA bandwidth, and receiver scheduling.

items.title: REAL-Q: E2E LLM Quantization via Dynamic Gradient Descent
items.one_sentence_takeaway: REAL-Q replaces one-shot layer solvers with block-wise gradient updates aligned to end-to-end output KL, improving 2-bit Qwen3-8B average zero-shot accuracy from 44.06% for the strongest listed baseline to 49.28%.
items.problem: Layer-wise PTQ freezes an approximate Hessian and drops cross-channel or cross-layer interactions, so its local reconstruction objective becomes misaligned as quantized columns accumulate.
items.why_it_matters: At 2–4 bits, small local errors compound through the network; preserving the full model's output distribution determines whether compressed weights remain deployable.
items.existing_approaches: RTN, GPTQ, GPTAQ, and GuidedQuant use closed-form or locally guided objectives that remain tractable by simplifying the global loss and typically solve a layer in one pass.
items.limitations: Dynamic gradients add calibration compute and memory, the paper reports quality rather than kernel or serving speed, and the theoretical descent condition is stated for SGD while experiments use Adam.
items.proposed_solution: Optimize an aggregated Fisher-MSE surrogate of end-to-end KL, refresh it after every 128-column block using gradient descent, and use a sliding loss window to smooth transitions between layers.
items.key_differences: The objective retains cross-output coupling and updates as the quantized model moves, rather than treating the original layer Hessian as valid for the whole solve.
items.results_with_conditions: LLaMA-3.1 8B/70B and Qwen3 0.6B–32B; QuaRot shared across baselines. W4A16 uses symmetric per-row weights with 2,048×2,048-token calibration except 70B uses 256 samples. Qwen3-8B W2A16, group 128, 256 samples: REAL-Q KL 49.9×10^-2, PPL 14.94, and 49.28% average over ten zero-shot tasks versus GPTAQ 60.6, 16.60, and 44.06%. W3A16 average is 65.50% versus GPTQ's 65.25%. GPU, batch, inference throughput, latency, and peak deployment memory were not reported in the primary source.
items.assessment: Promising algorithmic value and worth deep reading for quantization researchers. Production relevance is not established until calibration cost, checkpoint generation time, and compatible low-bit kernels are measured.

items.title: vLLM: Enable DSV3 GEMM for Strided Kimi-K3 Projections
items.one_sentence_takeaway: Accepting inner-contiguous row-strided inputs keeps four Kimi-K3 projection shapes on the DSV3 low-latency GEMM path, cutting measured B300 kernel time by 12.6–81.1%.
items.problem: Kimi-K3 projection slices were contiguous in their inner dimension but retained a wider row stride, causing vLLM to reject them and fall back to F.linear/NVJet.
items.why_it_matters: Low-M decode projections are launch- and shape-sensitive; an unnecessary fallback can dominate a branch even when the underlying data layout is safe for the tuned GEMM.
items.existing_approaches: The DSV3 kernel required fully contiguous tensors, so row-strided views were materialized through or executed by the generic linear path.
items.limitations: Only four BF16 microshapes were published on one B300; there is no end-to-end latency or throughput result, and the optimization is specific to the Kimi-K3 NVIDIA path.
items.proposed_solution: Relax the layout gate to accept inner-contiguous row-strided tensors and pass their stride correctly to the DSV3 low-latency GEMM without copying.
items.key_differences: The change expands eligibility based on the stride actually consumed by the kernel rather than imposing whole-tensor contiguity.
items.results_with_conditions: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 AC, BF16, CUDA-graph median of five repetitions. KDA f_b projection [M,N,K]=[1,1536,128]: 2.129→1.116 µs; M=4: 3.785→2.209; M=16: 2.827→2.472. MLA q_b [1,2304,1536]: 20.357→3.845 µs. Reductions span 12.6–81.1% versus F.linear/NVJet. Batch size corresponds to M; input/output sequence lengths, concurrency, memory, and end-to-end results were not reported.
items.assessment: A credible low-level fix with unusually clear shape data. Worth reproducing if serving Kimi-K3 on B300, but it should not be cited as a model-level speedup.
